units.title: Fluids
units.blurb: Pressure in still fluids, buoyancy, and the flow of moving fluids.

units.title: Thermodynamics
units.blurb: Gases, heat flow, the first and second laws, and engines.

units.title: Electric Force, Field and Potential
units.blurb: Charges, Coulomb's law, fields, potential and capacitors.

units.title: Electric Circuits
units.blurb: Current, resistance, power, series and parallel networks, Kirchhoff's rules and RC circuits.

units.title: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
units.blurb: Magnetic forces on moving charges and currents, fields of currents, and induction.

units.title: Geometric Optics
units.blurb: Mirrors and lenses: reflection, refraction and the images they form.

units.title: Waves, Sound and Physical Optics
units.blurb: How waves move, reflect and add, standing waves and sound, and the wave behavior of light.

units.title: Quantum Physics and the Nucleus
units.blurb: Photons, energy levels and spectra, matter waves, and the energy stored in nuclei.

topics.title: Pressure and Depth
topics.short: In a still fluid P = P₀ + ρgh, and gauge pressure leaves out the air pressure above.
topics.trouble: Students think a wider container makes the pressure at the bottom greater, when only the depth matters.

topics.title: Pascal's Principle and Hydraulics
topics.short: A pressure change spreads through a confined fluid, so a small force on a small piston lifts a heavy load.
topics.trouble: Students think a hydraulic lift gives energy for free, forgetting the small piston moves much farther.

topics.title: Buoyant Force and Archimedes' Principle
topics.short: The fluid pushes up with the weight of the fluid displaced, F_b = ρ_fluid·V·g, and a floating object displaces its own weight.
topics.trouble: Students think the buoyant force depends on the object's own weight or density instead of the volume of fluid it pushes aside.

topics.title: Flow Rate and Continuity
topics.short: For a liquid filling a pipe, the flow rate Av is the same everywhere: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
topics.trouble: Students think water slows down where a pipe gets narrower.

topics.title: Bernoulli's Equation
topics.short: Along a streamline P + ½ρv² + ρgh stays the same, so faster-moving fluid has lower pressure.
topics.trouble: Students think faster-moving fluid pushes harder, so its pressure must be higher.

topics.title: The Ideal Gas Law
topics.short: PV = nRT = Nk_BT, with the temperature in kelvins.
topics.trouble: Students use Celsius, so warming a gas from 20 °C to 40 °C seems to double its pressure.

topics.title: Temperature and Molecular Energy
topics.short: Each gas molecule has average kinetic energy (3/2)k_BT, so a monatomic gas holds internal energy U = (3/2)nRT.
topics.trouble: Students think every molecule in a gas moves at the same speed, or that heavier molecules at the same temperature carry more kinetic energy.

topics.title: Latent Heat
topics.short: Melting or boiling a mass m takes Q = mL; add the warming stages to find the total heat.
topics.trouble: Students forget the heat needed to melt the ice before the water can warm up.

topics.title: Rate of Heat Conduction
topics.short: Heat flows through a slab at the rate P = kAΔT/L, so thinner and wider walls pass more.
topics.trouble: Students think a good conductor must be hot, rather than a material that passes heat along quickly.

topics.title: Thermal Radiation and Blackbodies
topics.short: Every object radiates P = eσAT⁴, and hotter objects glow at shorter peak wavelengths: λ_max·T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K.
topics.trouble: Students think only glowing objects radiate, or that doubling the kelvin temperature doubles the radiated power instead of multiplying it by 16.

topics.title: Work Done on a Gas
topics.short: W = −PΔV is the work done on the gas, and its size is the area under the path on a P–V diagram.
topics.trouble: Students get the sign of the work wrong, mixing up the work done on the gas with the work done by it.

topics.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
topics.short: ΔU = Q + W: the internal energy changes by the heat added plus the work done on the gas.
topics.trouble: Students think adding heat must raise the temperature, forgetting the gas can spend that energy doing work.

topics.title: Isobaric, Isochoric, Isothermal and Adiabatic Processes
topics.short: Each process holds one thing fixed, which decides how Q, W and ΔU split.
topics.trouble: Students think an isothermal process has no heat flow, mixing it up with an adiabatic one.

topics.title: Cycles on a P–V Diagram
topics.short: Around a closed cycle ΔU = 0, and the area enclosed is the net work.
topics.trouble: Students add up the work of each leg without signs, so the net work comes out as the whole area under the paths.

topics.title: Heat Engines and Efficiency
topics.short: An engine turns part of the heat Q_H into work and gives off the rest as Q_C, with efficiency e = W/Q_H.
topics.trouble: Students think a well-designed engine could turn all of its heat into work.

topics.title: The Carnot Limit
topics.short: No engine running between T_H and T_C can beat e = 1 − T_C/T_H, with temperatures in kelvins.
topics.trouble: Students put Celsius temperatures into the Carnot formula.

topics.title: Refrigerators and Heat Pumps
topics.short: Work can move heat from cold to hot, and a heat pump delivers more heat than the work it uses.
topics.trouble: Students think a heat pump that delivers 3 J of heat for each joule of work breaks conservation of energy.

topics.title: Entropy and the Second Law
topics.short: Heat flows from hot to cold on its own; ΔS = Q/T, and the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
topics.trouble: Students think entropy can never go down anywhere, even inside a refrigerator.

topics.title: Charge, Conductors and Charging
topics.short: Charge comes in whole multiples of e and is conserved, and objects charge by friction, contact or induction.
topics.trouble: Students think a neutral object holds no charges at all, so nothing could attract it.

topics.title: Coulomb's Law
topics.short: F = k|q₁q₂|/r²: double the distance and the force drops to a quarter.
topics.trouble: Students think the larger charge feels the larger force.

topics.title: Adding Electric Forces
topics.short: The net force on a charge is the vector sum of the forces from each of the other charges.
topics.trouble: Students add the sizes of forces that point in different directions.

topics.title: The Electric Field
topics.short: E = F/q is the force on each coulomb; a point charge makes E = k|q|/r², pointing away from a positive charge.
topics.trouble: Students think the field at a point depends on the test charge placed there.

topics.title: Fields of Several Charges and Field Lines
topics.short: Add the field vectors from each charge; field lines show the direction, and their spacing shows the strength.
topics.trouble: Students think field lines are the paths charges must follow, or that two lines can cross.

topics.title: Charges in a Uniform Field
topics.short: Between parallel plates E is uniform, so a charge feels a constant force qE and moves like a projectile.
topics.trouble: Students forget that an electron is pushed opposite to the field.

topics.title: Electric Potential Energy
topics.short: Two charges store U = kq₁q₂/r, positive when they repel and negative when they attract.
topics.trouble: Students drop the signs of the charges, so attracting charges seem to store positive energy.

topics.title: Electric Potential and Voltage
topics.short: Potential is energy per charge, V = kq/r near a point charge, and a charge crossing ΔV gains or loses qΔV of kinetic energy.
topics.trouble: Students mix up potential (a scalar, energy per charge) with potential energy or with the field.

topics.title: Equipotentials and Field Strength
topics.short: The field points from high to low potential, at right angles to equipotentials, with E = ΔV/d between plates.
topics.trouble: Students think the field is zero wherever the potential is zero.

topics.title: Capacitors
topics.short: C = Q/V, and for parallel plates C = κε₀A/d.
topics.trouble: Students think a capacitor's capacitance depends on how much charge it holds.

topics.title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
topics.short: A charged capacitor stores U = ½QV = ½CV².
topics.trouble: Students use U = QV, forgetting the voltage grows from zero while the capacitor charges.

topics.title: Electric Current
topics.short: I = ΔQ/Δt, and conventional current points the way positive charge would flow.
topics.trouble: Students think current gets used up as it passes through a bulb.

topics.title: Resistance and Resistivity
topics.short: R = ρL/A, so longer and thinner wires resist more.
topics.trouble: Students think a thicker wire has more resistance because there is more metal in it.

topics.title: Power in Resistors
topics.short: P = IV = I²R = V²/R are three forms of one idea.
topics.trouble: Students conclude that a bigger resistor always uses more power, missing that in parallel the smaller one does.

topics.title: Resistors in Series
topics.short: One current passes through every resistor, the voltages add, and R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + ⋯.
topics.trouble: Students think the current gets smaller after each resistor in series.

topics.title: Resistors in Parallel
topics.short: Each branch has the same voltage, 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ⋯, and adding a branch lowers R_eq.
topics.trouble: Students think adding a resistor in parallel raises the total resistance.

topics.title: Series-Parallel Combinations
topics.short: Reduce a circuit step by step, then work back out to find each current and voltage.
topics.trouble: Students combine two resistors as if in series or parallel when they are neither.

topics.title: Kirchhoff's Junction Rule
topics.short: The current flowing into a junction equals the current flowing out, because charge is conserved.
topics.trouble: Students think the current always splits equally at a junction.

topics.title: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule
topics.short: The voltage changes around any closed loop add to zero, because energy is conserved.
topics.trouble: Students get the sign wrong when crossing a resistor against the current.

topics.title: EMF and Internal Resistance
topics.short: A real battery's terminal voltage is ε − Ir, so it sags as the current grows.
topics.trouble: Students think a battery always delivers the voltage printed on it.

topics.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel
topics.short: Parallel capacitances add, and series capacitances combine by reciprocals, the opposite of resistors.
topics.trouble: Students add series capacitances directly, as they would series resistors.

topics.title: RC Circuits
topics.short: A capacitor charges through a resistor with time constant τ = RC, and once full it blocks steady current.
topics.trouble: Students think an empty capacitor blocks current the moment the switch closes, when at first it acts like a plain wire.

topics.title: Magnetic Fields and Their Sources
topics.short: Magnets and moving charges make magnetic fields, measured in teslas, whose lines form closed loops.
topics.trouble: Students think magnetic field lines begin and end on poles, the way electric field lines begin and end on charges.

topics.title: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge
topics.short: F = qvB sin θ, at right angles to both v and B, by the right-hand rule.
topics.trouble: Students think a magnetic field pushes a charge along the field lines, or pushes a charge at rest.

topics.title: Charges Circling in a Magnetic Field
topics.short: The magnetic force is centripetal, so r = mv/(|q|B), and it never changes the speed.
topics.trouble: Students think the magnetic force speeds the charge up.

topics.title: Magnetic Force on a Current
topics.short: A wire carrying current I across a field B feels F = ILB sin θ.
topics.trouble: Students use the direction of electron flow in the right-hand rule instead of conventional current.

topics.title: Fields of Wires and Solenoids
topics.short: A long wire makes B = μ₀I/(2πr) in circles around it, a solenoid makes a nearly uniform B = μ₀nI inside, and parallel currents attract.
topics.trouble: Students expect parallel currents to repel, the way like charges do.

topics.title: Magnetic Flux
topics.short: Φ = BA cos θ counts the field passing through a loop, with θ measured from the loop's normal.
topics.trouble: Students measure the angle from the loop's plane instead of its normal.

topics.title: Faraday's Law
topics.short: A changing magnetic flux makes an emf: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt.
topics.trouble: Students think a strong but steady field makes an emf, when only a changing flux does.

topics.title: Lenz's Law
topics.short: The induced current makes a field that opposes the change in flux.
topics.trouble: Students think the induced field always points against the magnet's field, rather than against the change.

topics.title: Motional EMF
topics.short: A rod sliding along rails at speed v makes ε = BLv, and the force on the induced current slows the rod.
topics.trouble: Students forget the force on the induced current, which always opposes the rod's motion.

topics.title: Reflection and Plane Mirrors
topics.short: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and a plane mirror's image is as far behind it as the object is in front.
topics.trouble: Students think stepping back from a mirror lets you see more of yourself.

topics.title: Index of Refraction
topics.short: n = c/v: light slows in glass and water, and its wavelength shrinks while its frequency stays the same.
topics.trouble: Students think the frequency of light changes when it enters glass.

topics.title: Snell's Law
topics.short: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with angles measured from the normal.
topics.trouble: Students measure the angles from the surface instead of the normal.

topics.title: Total Internal Reflection
topics.short: Going from higher to lower n, light beyond the critical angle, sin θc = n₂/n₁, reflects completely.
topics.trouble: Students think total internal reflection can happen as light goes from air into glass.

topics.title: Curved Mirrors and Ray Diagrams
topics.short: Three principal rays locate the image formed by a concave or convex mirror.
topics.trouble: Students think covering half of a mirror removes half of the image, rather than dimming all of it.

topics.title: The Mirror Equation
topics.short: 1/f = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ and m = −dᵢ/dₒ, with signs that mark real and virtual images.
topics.trouble: Students drop the sign convention and give a convex mirror a positive focal length.

topics.title: Lenses and Ray Diagrams
topics.short: Converging and diverging lenses bend parallel rays toward or away from a focal point.
topics.trouble: Students think blocking half of a lens cuts off half of the image.

topics.title: The Thin Lens Equation
topics.short: The mirror equation works for lenses too, and real images form on the far side of the lens.
topics.trouble: Students forget that a diverging lens has a negative focal length.

topics.title: What Sets a Wave's Speed
topics.short: The medium sets the speed, v = √(tension/μ) on a string, and the source sets the frequency.
topics.trouble: Students think shaking a rope faster sends the waves along it faster.

topics.title: Snapshot and History Graphs
topics.short: A y–x graph shows the whole wave at one instant; a y–t graph follows one point over time.
topics.trouble: Students read the wavelength off a y–t graph, which really shows the period.

topics.title: Reflection at Boundaries
topics.short: A pulse reflects upside down from a fixed end and right side up from a free end, and partly passes into a new medium.
topics.trouble: Students think a reflected pulse always comes back the same way up.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Waves
topics.short: Light is a wave of linked electric and magnetic fields moving through empty space at c = fλ.
topics.trouble: Students think electromagnetic waves need a medium to travel through, or that radio waves are a kind of sound.

topics.title: Polarization
topics.short: Only transverse waves can be polarized; a polarizer passes half of unpolarized light and I₀cos²θ of polarized light.
topics.trouble: Students think no light can get through two crossed polarizers, even with a third one set at 45° between them.

topics.title: Superposition and Interference
topics.short: Overlapping waves add point by point: crest on crest builds up, crest on trough cancels.
topics.trouble: Students think two waves that cancel are destroyed, rather than passing through each other unchanged.

topics.title: Standing Waves on Strings
topics.short: A string fixed at both ends resonates at fₙ = nv/(2L).
topics.trouble: Students think a node is where the string moves the most.

topics.title: Standing Sound Waves in Pipes
topics.short: Open pipes resonate at fₙ = nv/(2L); pipes closed at one end only at odd multiples of v/(4L).
topics.trouble: Students give a pipe closed at one end the same set of harmonics as an open pipe.

topics.title: Sound Intensity and Decibels
topics.short: Intensity falls off as 1/r², and β = 10 log(I/I₀), so adding 10 dB means 10 times the intensity.
topics.trouble: Students think doubling the intensity doubles the decibel level.

topics.title: The Doppler Effect
topics.short: A source moving toward you sounds higher and one moving away sounds lower: f′ = f·v/(v ∓ vₛ).
topics.trouble: Students think the pitch keeps rising as an approaching source gets closer, when it stays steady and then drops as the source passes.

topics.title: Diffraction
topics.short: Waves spread out past an opening, and a single slit makes dark fringes where a sin θ = mλ.
topics.trouble: Students think a narrower slit makes a narrower central bright band, when it makes a wider one.

topics.title: Double-Slit Interference
topics.short: Bright fringes appear where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths: d sin θ = mλ.
topics.trouble: Students think moving the slits closer together squeezes the fringes closer, when it spreads them apart.

topics.title: Diffraction Gratings
topics.short: Many evenly spaced slits make sharp bright lines at d sin θ = mλ, where d is 1 divided by the number of lines per meter.
topics.trouble: Students use the number of lines per millimeter as d instead of its reciprocal.

topics.title: Thin-Film Interference
topics.short: Light reflecting from the top and bottom of a thin film interferes, with a half-wave flip at each reflection off a higher index.
topics.trouble: Students forget that the wavelength inside the film is λ/n, or miss a half-wave flip on reflection.

topics.title: Photons
topics.short: Light comes in photons of energy E = hf = hc/λ, and 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
topics.trouble: Students think brighter light has more energetic photons, rather than more of them.

topics.title: The Photoelectric Effect
topics.short: An electron escapes a metal only if a single photon brings more than the work function: Kₘₐₓ = hf − φ.
topics.trouble: Students think brighter light should give the electrons more energy, or that dim light just needs more time to work.

topics.title: The Bohr Model and Energy Levels
topics.short: Electrons in atoms have only certain energies, and a jump between levels absorbs or emits a photon whose energy is the difference between the two levels.
topics.trouble: Students think an electron gives off light the whole time it circles, or list only the jumps that end on the lowest level when counting possible lines.

topics.title: Emission and Absorption Spectra
topics.short: A hot thin gas emits bright lines, and the same gas in front of a hotter source absorbs those same lines.
topics.trouble: Students think a gas absorbs different colors from the ones it emits.

topics.title: Matter Waves
topics.short: Particles have a wavelength λ = h/p, so electrons diffract like light.
topics.trouble: Students think only light can act like a wave.

topics.title: Compton Scattering
topics.short: A photon carries momentum p = h/λ, so an X-ray that bounces off an electron comes away with a longer wavelength.
topics.trouble: Students think the scattered photon slows down, when it still moves at c and its lost energy shows up as a longer wavelength.

topics.title: Mass-Energy and Binding Energy
topics.short: E = mc²: a nucleus has less mass than its separate protons and neutrons, and the missing mass is its binding energy.
topics.trouble: Students think a nucleus should weigh more than its parts because it holds energy.
